opus-5.5.text:
Well, the hands thing is actually a really good example of what bothers me. For a long time the running joke was that these models couldn't count fingers, and now they mostly get five. People point to that as evidence the problem is solved. But I'd ask: *how* did it get solved? My suspicion is that it wasn't because the model suddenly developed an understanding of what a hand is, that it's a structured thing with bones and joints and a fixed number of digits. It's that we threw a lot more data and compute at it, and the statistical patch got good enough that the failure stopped showing up in the typical case.

That distinction matters. If you have a system that genuinely represents the structure of the world, then getting hands right should come for free, along with a whole bunch of other things. If instead you've just sanded down one very visible failure mode, you should expect the same kind of error to pop up somewhere else, somewhere less obvious, where nobody's thought to look yet. And that's roughly what you see. Objects pass through each other, things appear and disappear, physics goes slightly wrong over longer clips. It's the same disease with different symptoms.

So I'm not saying the outputs aren't impressive. They're stunning. What I'm skeptical of is the narrative that these models are learning "world models" just because the pixels look right. Looking right and being right are different things, and we've built an entire research culture that's really good at optimizing for the former. That's part of why I've become more interested in approaches that try to get the representation itself right, rather than just scaling until the artifacts become rare enough that we stop noticing them.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether five-fingered hands show real understanding, suggesting instead that more data and compute made a statistical fix work in typical cases.

r002.rationale: It says a system that represents a hand as a structured thing with bones, joints, and fixed digits should get hands right naturally.

r003.rationale: It argues that scaling can make artifacts rare enough that people stop noticing them, obscuring the underlying representation problem.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the five fingers thing is kind of the point, actually. Hands used to be the canonical failure mode, the thing everyone screenshotted, and now the models mostly get them right. But I don't think they got them right because they learned anything about hands. They got them right because the training data got bigger and the models got bigger, and the distribution of pixels that looks like a hand got sampled more densely. That's a different thing from understanding that a hand is a rigid structure with joints and a fixed number of digits.

And you can see the difference as soon as you move away from the thing that got fixed. The fingers are fine, but then someone picks up a cup and the cup passes through their palm, or they put it down and it's a slightly different cup, or there are two of them. Objects appear and disappear. Someone walks behind a pillar and comes out with different clothes. Those are the hands of two years ago, just further along the tail. So my worry is that we're playing whack-a-mole on the surface statistics and calling it progress toward a world model.

The deeper issue for me is what these models are actually being asked to do. They're trained to produce plausible frames, basically to be convincing. And "convincing" is a much weaker target than "correct." A physics engine gets physics right because it's got the physics in it. A video model gets physics right, when it does, because it saw enough examples of things falling that it can interpolate. The moment you ask for something slightly out of distribution, you find out how shallow that is. People put a lot of weight on the demos, but demos are selected, and the whole pipeline is optimised for the thing that looks good in a demo.

I'd also say, and this is maybe the more boring point, that I just don't think we should be too impressed by things that are easy to check with your eyes and hard to check for consistency. A human watching a clip for five seconds will catch six fingers immediately and completely miss that the shadows are wrong or that the room geometry changed. So the metric that got fixed was the one that was most visible to us, not the one that's most important. If anything, that makes me slightly more suspicious, not less, because it suggests the models are being tuned against the thing people complain about rather than toward anything like a consistent model of the scene.

That doesn't mean they're useless, they're obviously useful for all kinds of things. I just don't think the fingers tell us much about whether we're on the road to the thing people keep claiming we're on the road to.

r001.rationale: The response says larger models and more data can produce five-fingered hands through denser pixel-pattern learning, without learning the hand’s underlying structure.

r002.rationale: It describes a hand as a rigid structure with joints and a fixed number of digits, but does not say that representing it in a more human-like way would make finger counting easier.

r003.rationale: It says surface-level gains are being called progress toward a world model and that demos and visible metrics receive too much weight, conveying how scaling success can obscure deeper representation problems.

astra-6.text:
Well, getting five fingers right is progress, but it doesn’t necessarily tell us that the model understands what a hand is or how it works. It could just be getting better at reproducing the visual patterns in its training data. Those explanations can look very similar in a short, impressive clip.

What I’d want to see is whether it can maintain a consistent world as things happen: objects interacting, disappearing behind something and coming back, actions having consequences. And whether that holds up when you ask for something unusual, rather than something close to a familiar shot. I’m not saying video models can’t learn that. I’m skeptical that improving visual quality, by itself, demonstrates it.

r001.rationale: It says five-fingered hands do not show that the model understands hands and could instead reflect reproducing learned visual patterns, capturing the distinction between solving representation and learning the visible result.

r002.rationale: It does not suggest that a more human-like representation of a hand would make finger counting easier.

r003.rationale: It questions whether visual quality demonstrates understanding, but does not argue that scaling success makes representational problems easier to ignore.

sol-6.1.text: Well, getting five fingers right doesn’t really address my skepticism. You can get better and better at making something look plausible without necessarily learning why the world behaves the way it does. A video can look convincing for a few seconds, but does the model understand the underlying physics? Can it keep track of objects and cause and effect over time? That’s a much stronger claim than generating realistic-looking frames. I’m not saying these models can’t learn any of that, but I don’t think visual quality alone demonstrates it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says correct-looking hands do not demonstrate understanding of world behavior, but it does not address whether five fingers reflect a hand representation or brute-force learning of the finger count.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not suggest that a more human-like representation of a hand would make finger counting easier.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not discuss scaling success or how it could make underlying representation problems easier to ignore.
